method: Background research agent opened primary and reputable secondary sources; notes at /home/ubuntu/research/haiti-indemnity-notes.md

events.title: Charles X ordinance
events.text: Charles X’s ordinance offered recognition of Haiti’s independence on condition that Haiti pay 150 million francs in five equal annual installments, the first due 31 December 1825. It also halved entry and exit duties for ships and merchandise under the French flag.
events.correction: The 50% preference covered entry and exit duties on ships and merchandise under the French flag, not only import duties.

events.title: Baron de Mackau and the squadron
events.text: Baron de Mackau reached Haiti on 3 July aboard the frigate La Circé. A French force of 14 warships or brigs, carrying more than 500 cannon, was used as a show of force at Port-au-Prince.
events.correction: Accounts differ on arrival sequence: Marlene Daut says La Circé first arrived with two vessels and was joined later by 14 brigs; FOKAL says all 14 warships with 528 cannon arrived on 3 July; BnF describes a 500-cannon squadron approaching by 8 July.

events.title: Boyer accepts under threat
events.text: With a French squadron threatening a blockade, President Boyer accepted the ordinance’s conditions on 8 July according to the BnF account; the Senate registered his undertaking on 11 July.
events.correction: Some accounts give 11 July as the signing date; BnF and FOKAL place Boyer’s acceptance on 8 July and Senate registration on 11 July. Historians differ on how exclusively the fleet explains the decision.

events.title: The 30-million-franc loan
events.text: To meet the first installment, Haiti contracted a 30-million-franc loan on the French market. After bank commissions Haiti received only 24 million francs; the indemnity plus this financing became known as the ‘double debt.’
events.correction: Ternaux & Gandolphe solicited bids; a syndicate led by Jacques Laffitte concluded the underwriting on 4 November 1825.

events.title: Treaty of Peace and Friendship
events.text: The treaty signed at Port-au-Prince on 12 February 1838 confirmed Haiti as a free, sovereign, independent state. The associated settlement cut the unpaid indemnity balance to 60 million francs, payable over 30 years.
events.correction: The often-cited 90 million francs is the revised total (about 30 million already due or paid plus a 60-million-franc balance); NYT archival documentation specifies 60 million plus 700,000 francs still owed from the first installment.

events.title: Debt service and the national budget
events.text: By 1914, more than three-quarters of Haiti’s national budget was reportedly going to repay French banks.
events.correction: The 75% figure refers to the national budget, not national income.

events.title: Occupation era and National City Bank
events.text: During the U.S. occupation (1915–1934), debt service to North American and French banks was reported at about 40% of national income. National City Bank acquired the Banque Nationale de la République d’Haïti in 1922.
events.correction: The 40% estimate covers the occupation-era period through 1934, not only the 1920s.

events.title: Final remittance
events.text: A final remittance to National City Bank was made in 1947, about 122 years after the 1825 ordinance, ending U.S. financial control.
events.correction: 1947 ends the National City Bank chain; one scholarly account dates repayment of unrelated post-1875 loans to 1961.

events.title: The Ransom: about $560 million paid
events.text: The New York Times calculated payments of about 112 million francs over seven decades, roughly $560 million in 2021 dollars, and estimated long-term lost economic output of $21 billion to $115 billion.
events.correction: The 112.323 million francs combine 66 million direct indemnity, 41.124 million loan principal and interest, and 5.199 million late fees. The $21–115 billion range is counterfactual growth modeling (2.15% and 3.2% growth assumptions), not a measured transfer; one reviewing economist rejected the estimates.

events.title: Bicentenary statement
events.text: On the bicentenary, President Emmanuel Macron said France had imposed a very heavy financial indemnity and announced a mixed Franco-Haitian commission of historians to examine the shared past, including the 1825 indemnity’s impact, and recommend next steps to both governments.
events.correction: The Élysée statement announces a historians’ commission; it does not announce financial reparations.

macronQuoteFr: « Cette décision plaçait alors un prix sur la liberté d’une jeune Nation, qui était ainsi confrontée, dès sa constitution, à la force injuste de l’Histoire. »
macronQuoteEn: This decision placed a price on the freedom of a young Nation, which was thus confronted, from its very formation, with the unjust force of History.
macronQuoteEnNote: Translation of the French Élysée text; no official English Élysée text was located.
nuances: NYT’s $560 million converts its reconstructed payment series into 2021 dollars; its $21–115 billion range is counterfactual. The first 30-million-franc installment was about six times Haiti’s 1825 annual government revenue (NYT citing Beaubrun Ardouin); BnF describes the full 150 million francs as at least ten times annual revenue.
